name: Compounded semaglutide / microdosing GLP-1

lead: Compounded semaglutide has the same active ingredient as Ozempic or Wegovy but is prepared by a compounding pharmacy instead of the manufacturer. Microdosing means using less than the label amount, a practice seen in fat-loss and longevity circles, with the aim of lower appetite and body fat and a leaner face and physique with fewer side effects or lower cost.

Semaglutide activates GLP-1 receptors, which lowers appetite and slows stomach emptying. Approved semaglutide has strong trial results for weight loss at labeled doses. For microdosed or compounded versions, evidence is limited to a narrative review and early-stage registered trials.

paras: People get it from compounding pharmacies, often as multi-dose vials, and use amounts below the approved label. It is combined with diet changes and training, and results build over weeks to months.

Common effects are nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, abdominal pain and constipation. The FDA does not review compounded drugs for safety or effectiveness and has reported adverse events linked to dosing errors, off-label dosing, unapproved salt forms, improper shipping and counterfeit products.

chain: Lower body fat, leaner face and body
angle.text: Users take compounded or gray-market semaglutide, often at below-label amounts, to cut appetite and body fat for a leaner face and physique. Fat loss is established at approved doses in large trials, while the microdosing version has not been studied.

lead: People use compounded semaglutide and low-dose GLP-1 regimens to lose body fat, which in turn lets the jawline, cheekbones and midsection show more definition. Semaglutide acts on appetite and satiety, so users eat less and the scale moves; in approved-dose trials the weight loss has been large, and in looksmaxxing and fitness circles it is discussed as a cutting tool, sometimes combined with resistance training and high protein intake to keep muscle [1].

Compounded semaglutide is semaglutide, the active ingredient in the approved drugs Ozempic, Wegovy and Rybelsus, that a compounding pharmacy has prepared as a custom product rather than the manufacturer's branded pen or tablet. "Microdosing" GLP-1 refers to an informal practice in which people use amounts smaller than the doses on the approved label, often drawn from multi-dose vials, with the stated aims of reducing appetite and body fat with fewer side effects or lower cost.[1]

In the United States the FDA listed Ozempic and Wegovy as being in shortage starting in August 2022, and federal law allows compounding pharmacies to prepare versions of drugs on the shortage list under certain conditions.[1] The FDA does not review compounded drugs for safety or effectiveness, and it has published warnings about dosing errors, doses above the approved label, unapproved salt forms of semaglutide, counterfeit products and products sold "for research purposes."

Semaglutide at approved doses has been studied in large randomized trials for diabetes and obesity. Evidence about microdosed regimens is limited to a narrative review and registered trials that are early or not yet reporting; no published controlled trial has established the effects of low-dose compounded semaglutide on appearance or body composition.[2][3][4]

paras: Semaglutide is a GLP-1 receptor agonist: it stimulates glucose-dependent insulin release, suppresses glucagon and acts on appetite centers in the hypothalamus.[1] Approved versions are marketed as Ozempic (US approval in December 2017, for diabetes), Rybelsus (an oral tablet, September 2019) and Wegovy (for weight management, June 2021).[1]

A compounded product is made by a pharmacy for an individual prescription, usually as a vial of solution. Microdosing is not a regulatory category. In community use it describes using less than the labeled dose, sometimes also called a low-dose or maintenance approach.[2]

Wikipedia describes semaglutide as mimicking the hormone GLP-1: it stimulates insulin release and suppresses glucagon, which controls blood sugar, and it acts on appetite-regulating brain circuits and may improve leptin signaling.[1] Preclinical studies cited there also describe effects on fat metabolism, inflammation and autophagy.[1] It slows gastric emptying, which is one reason nausea and fullness are common early on.[1]

Because compounded versions contain the same active molecule when made from the correct form, these mechanisms apply to them in principle. The FDA draws a distinction for semaglutide sodium and semaglutide acetate, which it says are different active ingredients from those in approved drugs and that it knows of no lawful basis for using them in compounding.

Evidence on approved-dose semaglutide is substantial. According to Wikipedia, a phase III obesity trial in 1,961 adults with a BMI of 30 or more found average weight loss of about 14.9 percent at week 68 compared with about 2.4 percent on placebo, alongside lifestyle intervention [1]. A trial in 17,604 people with established heart disease reported about 18.8 percent fewer major adverse cardiovascular events than placebo over roughly 34 months [1]. A 2024 systematic review of six studies cited by Wikipedia found lean mass unchanged in some and significantly reduced in others, while lean-to-total mass ratios rose in every study [1]. After stopping, people on average regain about two thirds of the lost weight within a year, according to the same article [1].

For compounded products specifically, a retrospective real-world study of 94 people (81 women and 13 men, mean age about 47) in a commercial wellness programme receiving weekly compounded semaglutide with cyanocobalamin reported average weight loss of 4.11 kg (4.57 percent) after three months, with fat mass down by 2.67 kg and trunk fat down by 1.10 kg, along with smaller losses of lean mass (1.43 kg) and skeletal muscle (0.88 kg) [5]. An opinion from clinical pharmacists described limited data showing positive outcomes in small cohorts of compounded semaglutide and tirzepatide patients, alongside significant legal and safety concerns [6].

After stopping approved-dose treatment, Wikipedia cites a 2025 review finding that people regained about 67 percent of lost weight within a year.[1] No published study has compared weight maintenance on low-dose regimens with that figure, which is the setting in which some community members describe using smaller amounts.[2]

The FDA declared a shortage of Ozempic and Wegovy beginning in August 2022, and US compounding pharmacies may prepare versions of drugs on the shortage list if they meet certain conditions.[1] As of January 2026 the chief executive of Novo Nordisk cited up to 1.5 million US users of compounded GLP-1 drugs.[1]

The FDA states that compounded drugs should be used only when a patient's medical needs cannot be met by an approved drug, and that they should be prescribed by a clinician and filled by a state-licensed pharmacy. The agency says semaglutide sodium and semaglutide acetate are different active ingredients from those in approved drugs and that it knows of no lawful basis for their use in compounding. It also reports counterfeit Ozempic in the US supply chain and illegal online sales of products labeled "for research purposes."[1]

A 2025 review for health care providers described compounded semaglutide products as potentially lacking the quality controls historically seen with compounded formulations, with risks of dosing errors, and noted fraudulent batches worldwide [7]. A 2026 editorial in Annals of Pharmacotherapy noted that with the shortage of the innovator products resolved, compounding pharmacies can legally sell only unique products, such as different routes of administration or added ingredients, and that efficacy and safety of these formulations are largely unknown [8]. A 2025 retrospective cohort of 153,044 US primary care patients using semaglutide or tirzepatide found 8.2 percent used compounded formulations, with a rising share over time [9].

The FDA advises that red flags for problem products include deep discounts, no screening by a licensed clinician, mislabeling and pharmacy names that do not exist or that belong to licensed pharmacies that did not make the product. It says retatrutide and cagrilintide cannot lawfully be used in compounding, has issued warning letters to telehealth companies, API distributors and outsourcing facilities in that area, and has an import alert (66-80) aimed at GLP-1 active ingredients with quality concerns. For multi-dose vials the agency's guidance is to discard a vial within 28 days of first use and to use a new sterile needle and syringe for each dose, and it warns against products that arrive warm or without adequate refrigeration.

Regulators in Europe and the UK raised alarms about falsified Ozempic pens in late 2023, with the EMA and Reuters reporting on 18 October, the MHRA warning on 23 November and the FDA following on 21 December.[1] On 1 October 2024 the FDA published guidance on compounding for drugs on its shortage list, a compounding Q&A and a notice on unapproved GLP-1 drugs for weight loss.[1]

No completed controlled trial of compounded semaglutide or of microdosed GLP-1 regimens for appearance or body composition was found. A 2026 narrative review in Cureus summarized the rationale and reported benefits of GLP-1 microdosing across body systems, noting high demand and limited supply of approved GLP-1 drugs as a background factor.[2]

Registered trials include NCT07092605, an early phase 1 study of microdosed GLP-1 for health, quality of life and longevity measures (n = 150, enrolling by invitation, start date November 2024),[3] and NCT07588984, a planned cohort study of GLP-1 medication with behavioral health programs (n = 2,310, not yet recruiting).[4] Neither has published results.

For approved semaglutide, common adverse effects are nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, abdominal pain and constipation. They are mostly mild to moderate, dose-dependent and typically peak during dose escalation.[1] Rare events include gastroparesis and bowel obstruction.[1]

As of May 31, 2026 the FDA had received 990 adverse event reports for compounded semaglutide and over 730 for compounded tirzepatide, and notes that underreporting is likely and that causation is often unclear. The agency has received reports, some requiring hospitalization, linked to dosing errors by patients measuring their own doses and by clinicians miscalculating, and to doses above the label. It has also received complaints about products arriving warm, about multi-dose vial handling, and about labels naming pharmacies that do not exist. In October 2023 counterfeit Ozempic pens reportedly containing insulin were linked to hospitalizations in Europe.[1]

Wikipedia also lists gallstones, early worsening of diabetic retinopathy seen in initial trials and a boxed warning for thyroid C-cell tumors based on rodent studies, with contraindication for people with a personal or family history of medullary thyroid carcinoma or MEN2 [1]. A 2026 case report described a 50-year-old woman who developed angioedema requiring intubation after what she later reported was an accidental ten-fold higher first injection of compounded semaglutide; hospitalization was complicated by hypoglycemia, and she was discharged on day 7 [10]. A JAMA medical news article discussed safety concerns around compounded semaglutide and tirzepatide, including how clinicians can help prevent dosing errors [11].

On looksmax-oriented forums, GLP-1 drugs are discussed as tools for rapid fat loss and facial leaning, and gray-market or compounded sources are discussed alongside approved ones. Users on one forum have described combining a GLP-1 with other agents during a cut before a lean bulk, and others have asked whether to add extended fasting on top of semaglutide.

Wikipedia says GLP-1 research began in the 1970s, with Jens Juul Holst and Joel Habener identifying its effects in 1988, and describes Novo Nordisk developing liraglutide in 1998 and then semaglutide. Wikipedia lists approvals in the US (2017 for Ozempic, 2021 for Wegovy), Canada and the EU (2018), and Japan (2018) [1]. Worldwide shortages occurred in 2023 because of high demand, and compounded versions filled part of the gap [1]. US list prices are high and insurance coverage varies by country and insurer [1].

Microdosing attracted media attention in 2025; a Washington Post article titled "Microdosing GLP-1 drugs became a longevity 'craze'" was shared on Hacker News, where commenters disputed whether the amounts described in it were really microdoses, and discussed self-adjusting amounts [12]. Wikipedia cites an anthropological study of Danish patients in which people frequently adjust dosing and timing and work to keep access [1].

Semaglutide was the top-earning drug in US sales in 2023, at 38.6 billion dollars, according to Wikipedia, and Novo Nordisk's growth has significantly affected Denmark's economy and currency.[1] Generic versions are becoming available in India, Canada, Brazil and China, with patent expiry varying by country, and US patent protection runs no earlier than December 2031.[1] Wikipedia lists later approvals including an indication for noncirrhotic MASH with liver fibrosis (US, August 2025) and an oral version for weight management (US, December 2025).[1] Wikipedia's account of public interest runs from a November 2022 New York Times explainer on why Ozempic was drawing attention through 2024 reporting by NPR and others on compounding pharmacies and buying compounded Wegovy online.[1]

lore.intro: Low-dose GLP-1 use is discussed in fat-loss and longevity circles as a way to get appetite suppression at lower cost or with fewer side effects, often alongside other compounds.

claims.claim: Taking less than the labeled dose gives most of the appetite benefit with fewer side effects.
Compounded semaglutide is equivalent to the branded drug.
Combining GLP-1 use with extended fasting speeds fat loss.
Lifting, cardio, protein and fiber alongside a GLP-1 keep the weight loss lean.
A low dose can be used to keep weight off after the full course.
Vials sold online or labeled for research are the same as pharmacy products.
GLP-1 drugs are a route to a leaner face as well as a leaner body.
